planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out once nights stay above 55F. A heavy-yielding sweet banana type, it tends to set long tapering fruit in flushes, so steady feeding and even moisture keep plants producing through summer.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping soil warm for even germination, then harden off and transplant after nights stay reliably above 55F. Space plants 18-24 inches apart in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and stake or cage to support the heavy fruit load. Pick the elongated yellow banana-type pods once they reach full size for the mildest, sweetest flavor; frequent picking encourages continued flowering and extends the harvest.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed. A thin-skinned slicing type bred for low bitterness, it benefits from a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean.

directions: Direct sow once soil temperature is reliably above 70F, planting several seeds per hill and thinning to the strongest vine, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for a jump on the season. Train vines up a trellis to save space and produce straighter fruit, and keep soil evenly moist to prevent bitterness and misshapen cucumbers. Harvest regularly while fruit are still slender since the thin, tender skin needs no peeling but turns tougher if left to oversize.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this compact, container-friendly habit still produces full-sized beefsteak fruit, making it a good choice for patios and small-space gardens.

directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a large container or garden bed once danger of frost has passed. Despite its compact, patio-friendly size, this determinate variety sets large beefsteak-style fruit, so provide a sturdy stake or small cage and consistent watering to prevent blossom end rot. Feed regularly through the season since container-grown plants exhaust soil nutrients faster than in-ground plantings.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; bred for strong downy mildew and fusarium resistance, it holds up well in variable spring weather.

directions: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in spring, or again in late summer for a fall harvest, covering seed lightly and keeping it evenly moist until germination. Thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart and harvest outer leaves continuously once plants reach usable size, which encourages a longer productive period before the plant eventually bolts in warm weather. Its strong disease resistance makes it a dependable choice for gardeners who have struggled with downy mildew on spinach in the past.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following the last frost; an improved take on the classic Blue Lake bean bred for heavier pod set and better disease tolerance.

directions: Direct sow once soil has warmed to at least 65F after the last frost, planting seeds an inch deep and spacing plants 3-4 inches apart in rows. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pod set to maximize yield, and pick pods while still slender and snappy for the best texture. This improved Blue Lake type is bred for rust, curly top, and mosaic virus resistance and holds its quality through a heavier flush of pods than the traditional Blue Lake 274 strain.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring and succession-sow every couple weeks; also suitable for a late-summer sowing for fall harvest.

directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning seedlings to about an inch apart so roots have room to size up without crowding. Keep the bed evenly moist, since inconsistent watering is the main cause of cracked or pithy roots in fast-growing radishes. This organic F1 hybrid matures quickly and uniformly, making it a good candidate for repeated succession sowings through spring and again in early fall.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for fall harvest; a red-pigmented sport of traditional tatsoi grown both for baby greens and mature rosettes.

directions: Direct sow in early spring or again in late summer, thinning to 6-10 inches apart for full rosettes or growing tighter for a cut-and-come-again baby-green harvest. The deep red-purple leaves intensify in cooler weather and hold their color well in salads or quick saute. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole rosette at the base once it reaches full size, and expect the plant to bolt once daytime temperatures climb in late spring.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost after a cold, moist pretreatment to improve germination; this compact strain sends up fragrant blush-pink flower spires that draw bees and other pollinators.

directions: Chill seed in moist sand or a damp paper towel in the refrigerator for a week before sowing to break dormancy, then start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or direct sow in fall in mild climates. Transplant into well-drained soil, since lupines resent soggy roots, and stake tall spires in windy spots. Expect first bloom the following year on perennial plantings, with the dense, scented flower spikes attracting bees throughout early summer.

planting.note: Plant tubers after the danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; part of the long-lasting Karma series bred specifically for cut-flower vase life.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally about 4-6 inches deep once the soil has warmed after the last frost, waiting to water heavily until sprouts emerge to avoid rot. Stake plants early since the Karma series grows vigorously and produces long, sturdy stems prized for cutting. In zones below 8, lift and store tubers indoors over winter after the first light frost blackens the foliage, dividing clumps before replanting the following spring.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; part of the Potomac series bred as a tall, uniform snapdragon for cut-flower production in field or greenhouse.

directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, barely covering the fine seed and keeping it cool for even germination. Transplant out once seedlings are hardened off and nighttime temperatures stay above freezing, since snapdragons tolerate light frost but not hard freezes. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching, stake or net the tall stems for support, and harvest spikes when the lower third of florets have opened for the longest vase life.
